title: After prime squares, more digits at the same primes buy less than another 4×
impact: For any finite set of odd primes coprime to the product, more than a quarter of the sums passing their squares still pass at any chosen higher precisions.
scope: A universal bound on fractions over the complete joint period. A short interval or a new prime can change the outcome. The example 94,579 reaches a 3.6466–3.6467× reduction.
detail: At each odd prime the extra reduction is bounded explicitly. Multiplying those bounds over any selection stays below four, however large the selected primes are.

title: The full prime-square pattern on the fresh product fits in 90,720 offsets
impact: Removing exact repetition cuts the list for one period from 29.3 billion offsets to 90,720 on the fresh product and from 20.1 billion to 8,279,040 on the crossed product.
scope: Two published 2,048-bit products and seven fixed prime-square tests. These are storage savings for a list of offsets. The number of surviving sums across the full interval stays the same.
detail: The proof certifies the shortest possible repeat in integer sums for each pattern. Separate per-prime tables can store the same tests using 101 and 485 bits before padding.

title: Using prime squares also saves about 26% and 29% of the small lookups
impact: Compared with the already reordered seven-prime scan, seven ordered prime-square checks take 25.52% fewer lookups on the fresh product and 29.17% fewer on the crossed product.
scope: Full public factor-width intervals on two 2,048-bit examples. Each reached table costs one lookup. The count excludes setup and machine-dependent costs.
detail: Both the number of small lookups and the number of final integer square tests fall. The smaller scan still needs about 8.51 × 10³⁰⁵ small lookups.

title: Applying the same polynomial to both factors adds no rejection at the same modulus
impact: Any sum that admits a modular factor pair also admits the transformed pair. If the linear coefficient of the polynomial remainder is a unit, both tests give exactly the same answer.
scope: Every common polynomial, including at even and composite moduli. The transformed sum and product are calculated from the same proposed sum and product.
detail: The false candidate 402 on 40,309 fails modulo 9. After squaring both factors, the transformed pair 2 and 2 passes modulo 9.

title: Seven prime squares cut the remaining sums by another 6.42× and 13.87×
impact: Measured from the initial modulo-four list, about one sum in 802 survives on the fresh product and one in 1,169 on the crossed product.
scope: Two published 2,048-bit comparison products with known factor widths. These figures count candidates that still need an integer square test. The smaller list contains at least 2¹⁰⁰⁶ sums.
detail: The seven odd primes range from 3 to 19. Their squared moduli give exact counts in each repeating block, which also bound the count across the actual interval.

title: Adding a check modulo 9 isolates the sum through 23 for every nine-bit prime pair
impact: Ordinary prime tests needed to reach 41 in the hardest case. With 9 included, 23 sufficed for all 903 distinct nine-bit pairs and all 253 eight-bit pairs.
scope: Complete populations at these two small factor widths. Only the product and factor widths enter each search. The known primes check the returned sum.
detail: For 136,831, the false guess 748 passes the ordinary primes through 37. Its discriminant is 3 modulo 9, which rules it out. Modulo 11 then leaves only 760, giving 293 and 467.

title: Every power of every prime through 19 still admits over 2⁹⁹⁸ wrong sums
impact: Inside the interval fixed by the factor widths, more than 2⁹⁹⁸ false sums on the fresh product and 2¹⁰⁰⁰ on the crossed product meet all these local conditions simultaneously.
scope: Two published 2,048-bit products. The count includes powers of 2 as well as all seven odd primes and removes the genuine sum.
detail: The proof counts whole classes of guesses that have a modular factor pair at every precision. Distinct guesses in these classes give distinct sums.

title: Changing test order saves about a quarter of the small lookups at 2,048 bits
impact: Across the full candidate interval, seven primes in order of their passing fractions save 24.5362–24.5363% of the lookups on the fresh product and 24.5833–24.5834% on the crossed product.
scope: Two previously published synthetic products. The proof counts an exhaustive scan from public widths and residue tables. Both reordered scans still exceed 10³⁰⁶ lookups.
detail: The final square tests are identical in both orders. Period counts and a rigorous bound for the last incomplete period give the totals without scanning the full interval.

title: Ascending prime order already minimizes lookups in 2 of 128 residue patterns
impact: For the seven odd primes through 19, sorting saves work in 126 patterns. The smallest positive saving is 180 lookups per full period and the largest is 2,992,699.
scope: Uniform phases in a full period, equal cost per lookup and a product coprime to all seven primes. Each pattern contains exactly 12,960 invertible residues.
detail: Both ties occur when the product is a nonsquare at every prime through 17. The result inventories residue classes and makes no sampling assumption about large prime factors.

title: Reordering the same 13 tests saved 3,495 lookups on the 39-bit product
impact: Sorting the public residue tables by how many residues pass reduced the scalar scan from 16,226 to 12,731 lookups. The sole survivor was again 1,310,542.
scope: One previously published product of two 20-bit primes. Both orders start with 7,273 candidates and apply the same tests to the survivors. The order uses only the small public tables.
detail: The saving is 21.54% in candidate–prime lookups. Sorting 13 fractions adds setup work. On one partial interval, interchanging two of the tests saves another 24 lookups.

title: One more reading settles the ambiguous four-position case
impact: Given all six counts and the first two tests at each position, one check of the third test identifies the joint hit or proves the window empty.
scope: Four positions with three tests and an ambiguous common count. The result supplies no inexpensive procedure for obtaining the six counts on a large interval.
detail: For w positions with k earlier tests mapped, the smallest of their groups contains at most floor(w/2ᵏ) positions. Reading that group and using the supplied margins recovers the joint count.

title: Two products give identical pair counts and different common-sum answers
impact: In the first four candidate sums, each prime test passes twice and each pair passes together once. For 10,961, one sum passes all three. For 187,709, none does.
scope: Two small semiprimes selected to compare the same residue tables at 3, 13 and 11. Both windows start at the lower end allowed by their product and balance bounds.
detail: The difference appears in the positions that pass modulo 13. Retaining the six counts alone discards this information.

title: Six counts determine the exact number of joint hits at 405 of 429 starts
impact: The counts force zero common hits in 275 windows, one in 128 and two in 2. In the 24 ambiguous windows the actual answers split evenly between zero and one.
scope: A complete period for four consecutive allowed sums when the product is 665 modulo 1,716. The percentage is over starting positions for that residue, with all six counts supplied.
detail: Sharp lower and upper bounds describe every answer consistent with three individual counts, three pair counts and the window length.

title: Every pair of tests can pass somewhere in an empty search interval
impact: On 34,387 the first three permitted sums each pass a different pair of the tests modulo 3, 13 and 11. None passes all three.
scope: A prefix at the actual lower end of this product’s balanced interval, using its public modulo-four condition. Every proper subset of the tests has a witness in that prefix.
detail: The first joint survivor is the fifth candidate, 388. Knowing just that each pair has some witness loses the positions needed to find a joint witness.

title: Remainder tests single out one full-size sum without assuming RH
impact: For any product of two 1,024-bit primes, the true sum is the only candidate in the stated public range that passes every odd prime through 2⁹⁴⁰.
scope: The proof uses the product and factor widths. It deductively applies three published unconditional inequalities, supplied as hypotheses in Lean.
detail: Visiting the entire family once would take more than 2⁹³⁰ prime visits. Finding the unique passing sum cheaply remains open.

title: The number of copies of a prime predicts its first rejecting power
impact: If d is a nonsquare modulo an odd prime and x contains that prime exactly a times, the test on d × x² first fails at exponent 2a + 1.
scope: Applies to a proposed discriminant with the stated decomposition. The example uses 9,523 = 89 × 107 and a deliberately wrong sum of 200.
detail: The example gives 1,908 = 53 × 6². Although 53 already fails modulo 3, the original discriminant passes modulo 3 and 9. It fails modulo 27.

title: Remainders through 43 recover the 39-bit factors without a clue
impact: The public width gives 7,273 possible sums after the modulo-four check. Three pass the primes through 41, and only 1,310,542 survives 43. This gives 556,559 × 753,983.
scope: One previously published seeded product of two 20-bit primes. The filters receive the product and factor width. The disclosed primes appear in the final verification.
detail: A direct staged scan uses 16,226 small remainder lookups. The Lean proof checks the complete sequence of counts with bit masks. This example establishes no success rate on larger inputs.

title: Small remainders cut the full-size sum counts about 125-fold and 84-fold
impact: Against the modulo-four count, testing the odd primes through 19 reduces the number of final square tests by a factor between 124.73 and 124.74 on the fresh control, and between 84.19 and 84.20 on the crossed control.
scope: Two published 2,048-bit products, using only each product and its factor widths. The counts cover visiting the whole allowed interval. Both have more than 2¹⁰⁰⁰ surviving sums.
detail: The proof counts complete periods and bounds the last partial period. The ratio measures the reduction in candidate count. Generating candidates and constructing small residue lists have their own costs.

title: A product-only sieve leaves at most 2⁵¹⁹ sums over the full factor-width interval
impact: Among 2¹⁰²⁴ consecutive sums covering two 1,024-bit primes, checking odd primes through 2⁵²⁰ retains the true sum and leaves at most 2⁵¹⁹ candidates.
scope: Unconditional for every pair in the stated bit widths. There are more than 2⁵¹¹ test primes. The theorem bounds survivors and leaves their efficient enumeration open.
detail: The proof specializes Gallagher’s classical larger sieve and establishes explicit finite constants for these factor-sum remainders.

title: Three prime powers allow a still coarser clue while keeping fewer than a million sums
impact: At 2,048 bits, a supplied interval total accurate to 2¹⁰⁵³ leaves at most 907,200 sums. This permits eight times the error of the earlier 635,040-candidate bound.
scope: Moduli 16, 9, 25, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19. The product and factor widths give the public constraints. The estimate for the individual product remains a separate input.
detail: The combined modulus exceeds the full diameter of the possible sums at this accuracy. Each admissible residue can therefore appear at most once.

title: Small remainders let the interval clue tolerate 32 times more error
impact: An error allowance of 2¹⁰⁵⁰ leaves at most 635,040 possible sums at 2,048 bits. The previous modulo-four bound gave at most 1,048,576 at an allowance of 2¹⁰⁴⁵.
scope: Any product of two distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. The remainder checks use the product alone. The interval-total estimate is supplied.
detail: Only 90,720 residues at most can be sums in a block of length 19,399,380. At this error allowance seven blocks cover every candidate, including partial blocks.

title: Remainders modulo 3 and 5 select the correct sum from five
impact: On 419,636,024,497, only 1,310,542 survives both checks. On the fresh and crossed 2,048-bit controls, the public remainders give conditional upper bounds of 272,160 and 403,200 sums.
scope: The 39-bit input used a deliberately noisy clue derived from its factors. The large-input figures assume an interval-total estimate accurate to 2¹⁰⁵⁰. No such reading was obtained on either control.
detail: Each large product determines exactly how many sum residues survive in one complete block. Multiplying that count by seven covers the possible interval.

title: Two square roots give direct access to every sum allowed by the reading
impact: For the 39-bit example the interval runs from 1,310,536 to 1,310,554. The first sum of the correct remainder is 1,310,538 and the fifth is 1,310,554.
scope: The calculation takes a supplied signed integer reading and a nonnegative error allowance. It also handles empty intervals and exact-square endpoints.
detail: Once the endpoints are known, adding four times a zero-based index to the first candidate gives the selected sum without visiting the preceding candidates.

title: Two interval readings can cancel the same unknown error
impact: On 143, adding 1,000 to both readings still recovers the prime sum 24. At 1,024-bit factor width, five publicly known lengths are always suitable for taking two readings.
scope: The measurements are supplied. If an unknown bias changes linearly with the length, every proposed sum fits the interior readings after refitting the slope and offset.
detail: A difference of totals retains a linear term in the factor sum. Two additional reference readings at lengths zero and one calibrate an affine error if that law holds globally.

title: Four gcds measure the change in slope, which is constant in the useful interval
impact: At 143 the successive measurements are −18, −22 and 2. The first two already sample gcds of 11 and 13. Inside the interval where the sum formula holds, the measurement is always 2.
scope: Four gcds of the product suffice for the second difference at every nonnegative length. The constant result applies when all three lengths include both prime contributions and lie below the smaller prime.
detail: Taking two differences cancels the linear term that carries the factor sum. The calculation pinpoints what this inexpensive product-only observation can reveal.

title: A deliberately noisy clue leaves five sums on the 39-bit example
impact: With an error allowance of 16 million, five sums remain. Only 1,310,542 gives a square discriminant and the primes 556,559 and 753,983.
scope: The disclosed factors of the seeded product 419,636,024,497 supplied the exact interval total. We added five million before giving the estimate to the sum test.
detail: The proof certifies the exact signed total, its perturbation, the full list of five candidate sums, and the resulting factorization.

title: A specified error in the interval total bounds the remaining search
impact: An absolute error of at most 2¹⁰⁴⁵ leaves at most 1,048,576 sums at 2,048 bits. At error 2¹⁰²⁵ only the correct sum survives when the estimate meets its guarantee.
scope: The decoder receives an integer estimate for the individual product. The true sum is in the list for balanced distinct odd primes.
detail: Legal sums differ by multiples of four. Their predicted totals get farther apart as the sum grows, which bounds how many can fit in one error interval.

title: A coarser supplied total can still locate the smaller prime
impact: With an estimate accurate to 2¹⁴⁵⁰, an explicit real number is within 2⁴⁷⁰ of the smaller prime except on fewer than one in 32,768 eligible pairs.
scope: Uniform sorted pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. The location uses the supplied estimate, and the bound is a radius.
detail: The calculation estimates the sum first, then takes its smaller real root. The gap between the actual primes controls the loss of accuracy in this second step.

title: Even a menu of 2⁶⁴ fixed multipliers almost always misses the interval total
impact: The best prediction cN from such a menu reaches the decoding tolerance on fewer than one in 2⁴¹⁸ eligible pairs. A single coefficient reaches it on fewer than one in 2⁴⁸².
scope: Coefficients are arbitrary real numbers fixed before seeing the prime pair. The choice among menu entries can use the entire product.
detail: Each successful coefficient predicts the sum using one fixed factor ratio. Counting the larger primes that can fit around that ratio limits the coverage.

title: The complete gcd average always decodes to the wrong sum at full size when used for the short interval
impact: At 143 the substitution gives a sum of 20, while the primes add to 24. Its downward error in the interval total is at least half the squared interval length for balanced primes of size at least 11.
scope: This tests replacing the triangular interval average by the exact mean over the whole modulus. At every balanced 2,048-bit input this specific substitution fails.
detail: The complete mean has an exact divisor formula and itself contains the factor sum. Extrapolating it to the short interval introduces the error.

title: Four clues still leave at least 2⁴⁷⁴ sums after enforcing both factor widths
impact: Except on fewer than one in 4,096 eligible prime pairs, at least 2⁴⁷⁴ sums pass all four square-divisor clues with both real roots inside the exact factor-width limits.
scope: Uniform sorted pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. A second guarantee of 2¹⁸⁶ sums has an exceptional fraction below 2⁻⁴⁴.
detail: The count allows the largest possible square divisor at each sign. The roots of a surviving candidate can be nonintegral.

title: One exact character average determines the sum of the primes
impact: At 143, the even-family average is 51/25. It gives the sum 24 and the factors 11 and 13. The same formula holds for every product of distinct primes greater than eight.
scope: The input to the decoder is an exact average over primitive even Dirichlet characters. At 2,048 bits, candidate sums four apart predict averages less than 2⁻⁴⁰⁸⁷ apart.
detail: Even the size of the family determines the factors. The proof leaves open how to obtain the average cheaply from the product alone.

title: Ninety-sixth powers still cancel at the small character inputs
impact: At every even power through 96, the difference between the even and odd totals is determined entirely by the supplied weights.
scope: Two distinct 1,024-bit primes. Every character input from 1 through 2²¹ is allowed, with arbitrary complex weights. The signed totals are unnormalized.
detail: Normalization preserves a small signal. With up to 2²¹ weights, moving between two candidate sums four apart changes the predicted normalized even mean by at most 2⁻⁴⁰⁶⁷ times the total squared weight.

sources.label: Connection to the GRH input range

title: One longer character sum at a public length determines the factors
impact: On 143 the interval length is eight. Its signed total is −44, and every integer reading from −96 through 23 still gives the correct factor sum 24 after rounding.
scope: Distinct primes p < q < 2p. The interval length is the integer part of √(N/2), at least 2¹⁰²³ for a full 2,048-bit product.
detail: For a balanced 2,048-bit product, an approximation within 2¹⁰²⁵ of the exact total suffices. Obtaining such an approximation cheaply remains open.

title: Random sampling almost always misses the terms that carry the factors
impact: At 2,048 bits, even 2⁶⁴ independent draws have probability at most 2⁻⁹⁵⁸ of seeing a term that differs from one.
scope: Uniform draws with replacement from the ordered index pairs in the long character sum. At 143, ten of the 64 pairs carry a changed term.
detail: A pair changes the total only when its index sum equals p or q. Grouping by that index sum gives a direct gcd calculation with 2B−1 diagonals at interval length B.

title: Four supplied square divisors usually leave at least 2⁵¹⁴ possible sums
impact: All four clues leave at least 2⁵¹⁴ compatible sums except on a fraction below 2⁻¹³. The lower bound of 2²⁵⁸ sums holds with an exceptional fraction below 2⁻⁴⁵.
scope: Uniform sorted pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. Compatible sums pass the basic balanced interval, the true remainder modulo four, two sum congruences and two discriminant congruences.
detail: One same-sign clue leaves at least 2⁷⁶⁴ sums, or one mixed-sign clue leaves at least 2⁷⁶⁷ gaps, except on a fraction below 2⁻⁷⁷. A candidate still needs an integer square discriminant to give factors.

title: One supplied square divisor fixes the sum on a 39-bit product
impact: The sum of the factors of 419,636,024,497 must lie among 78,590 integers. Knowing that 288² divides (p+1)(q+1) leaves only 1,310,542, giving the primes 556,559 and 753,983.
scope: First seeded draw of two distinct 20-bit primes. Their disclosed factors supplied the four largest square divisors used as clues.
detail: The sum is 66,382 modulo 82,944. Exactly one integer in the balanced window has that remainder, and its discriminant is 197,424².

title: Even more guesses than possible smaller factors almost never reach a working scale
impact: Giving all four sign choices every scale through 2¹⁰²⁴ reaches fewer than one in 2⁴⁶² eligible prime pairs. A trillion-scale budget reaches fewer than one in 2⁹⁵⁹.
scope: Uniform sorted pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. The bound allows product-dependent choices within the entire budget.
detail: Counting both neighboring integers together bounds how many products can be a small integer times a square. Even with a scale cap of 2¹⁷⁹² the fraction is below one in 2⁷⁷.

title: Every sign and every scale through a trillion fails on both full-size controls
impact: The fresh and crossed 2,048-bit products each have a Lean certificate ruling out all four sign choices at every positive scale through 2⁴⁰.
scope: These are retrospective checks with known factors. The fresh certificate also uses two primes disclosed by its construction.
detail: On the fresh successor product, odd prime multiplicities left 4,197 possible multipliers. Small-prime square tests ruled out all 4,197. The crossed successor product left 3,693, all excluded as well.

title: One square-root guess can test four links between the two factors
impact: On all 32,385 pairs of distinct 12-bit primes the four-sign scan found 1,343 products. The two-sign comparison found 661 on the same per-product square-root allowances.
scope: Bounded census through scale 16. Fermat found 14,500 products on matched budgets, including 14,076 missed by the four-sign scan. The four-sign scan alone found 919.
detail: The even neighbors of odd primes force an even root at every successful squarefree scale. One scaled square suffices for all four signs at scales two and above. The two readings yield either a candidate sum or a candidate gap.

sources.label: Why only one square test can survive

title: One scaled root checks both sides of the product
impact: Across all 32,385 products of distinct 12-bit primes, trying both signs through scale 16 found 638 products. Trying the predecessor alone found 321.
scope: The candidate-selection proof applies to balanced factors. Ordinary Fermat search found 13,818 of these products on matched square-root budgets, with 463 found only by the two-sided scan.
detail: Each scale produces two possible sums. Comparing them selects the only one that can pass the balanced interval, so each scale needs at most one discriminant root. More scales can reach that last test than in the one-sided scan.

title: Two impossible factor remainders can rule out a whole family of guesses
impact: On 2,627 no squarefree multiple of 13 can be the first successful scale. Its two possible remainders modulo 169 both miss the smaller-factor interval.
scope: For a guessed prime divisor of the squarefree predecessor scale. Checking small primes saved six scaled roots on 2,627, while ordinary interval trial division found its factor in one division.
detail: The same odd-interval screen reduced 371 scaled roots to 315 on 3,713 and 524 to 483 on 4,757, in return for additional divisibility checks.

title: One weighted sum detects which prime’s sequence repeats
impact: At shift ten on 143 the first weighting incorrectly signaled a full repeat. The second weighting gave 77, whose gcd identifies 11 as the only prime with a repeat.
scope: The second weighting works for all products of distinct primes at least eleven. The calculation checks a proposed shift and still needs a full sum in the direct implementation.
detail: The first weighting has a single exceptional prime, 13. Moving the two readings one position forward and choosing coefficients 3 and −10 gives an exact test for both factors.

title: The product’s square root picks one degree that reveals a factor
impact: On 493 the chosen degree is 22. The discrepancy gives 29, and the ordinary binomial coefficient gives 17.
scope: For distinct odd primes with the larger less than twice the smaller. Computing the complete sum directly visits every residue. Twin primes have a separate square test for the coefficient method.
detail: The degree is the largest even integer at or below the square root of the product. The same discrepancy gives the larger prime at every even degree between the two prime predecessors, including the lower endpoint.

title: One weighted sum recovers the larger prime without a binomial coefficient
impact: On 2,627 the sum gave 355, which shares the factor 71 with the product. It used 2,414 modular powers in place of 4,828 for the two separate sums.
scope: The primes are at least seven, their gap is at least six and the larger is less than twice the smaller. Gaps of two and four have direct square tests.
detail: This input was chosen because the first Fermat test misses. Fermat still found 37 in three square tests, and the direct Jacobi scan had already exposed 37 on its 36th sign.

title: Two consecutive readings decide whether every later reading repeats
impact: On 119 a false shift can give the correct first value, 2, or the correct second value, 6. Getting both values certifies a repeat for the whole sequence.
scope: Every product of two distinct primes at least seven. This checks a proposed shift. Obtaining the two readings directly still takes a pass over all residues.
detail: The multipliers in the usual recurrence of consecutive middle binomial coefficients distinguish the starting position from every other interior position. The proof checks the two endpoints separately.

sources.label: What the two readings tell us

title: Some prime pairs give no factor from a raw even moment at any degree
impact: On 65 every positive even degree has gcd one. On 77, four degrees gave all four possible gcds, 1, 7, 11 and 77.
scope: An exact classification for distinct odd prime factors. A prime appears in the gcd precisely when it is 3 modulo 4 and one less than the prime divides the degree.
detail: The 14 control readings used 157 signs and 770 modular powers. The signs for a product were reused across its degrees.

title: On the fresh comparison the first successful scale exceeds 2¹⁰⁷⁹
impact: That first guess is larger than the smaller prime itself. On the crossed comparison the first successful scale exceeds 2⁶⁴. Both inputs exceed the trillion-guess budget.
scope: These two retrospective certificates use the published prime factors. The fresh input’s prime construction supplied two additional certified divisors. Exact first scales remain unknown.
detail: Primes occurring an odd number of times in the totient must divide every successful scale. The shortest shared periods on the fresh and crossed controls have 2,046 and 1,439 bits, respectively.

sources.label: Why odd multiplicities give a bound

title: The product can rule out a whole class of guesses before the first square root
impact: For 3,713, its first successful scale cannot be even or divisible by 29. The product-dependent check cut the remaining scale roots from 574 to 371.
scope: The proof concerns squarefree guesses, including the first successful scale of a balanced semiprime. At 221 the check saved zero roots. Elapsed-time savings remain unmeasured.
detail: At 4,757 it reduced 740 scale roots to 524 with an additional 2,220 candidate modulus tests. Both searches used the same balanced-sum window and returned the same factor.

sources.label: When the product rules out a scale

title: A fixed table skips 36% of square-root guesses in each full block
impact: On 4,757 the same first factor appeared at guess 1,155, using 740 scale roots and 706 discriminant roots. The earlier scan used 1,155 and 1,104.
scope: The first correct scale is squarefree for balanced prime pairs. The table skips multiples of 4, 9 and 25, and works at any positive search cap.
detail: Exactly 576 of every 900 aligned guesses remain. Building the reusable table cost 2,175 small divisibility checks in the experiment.

sources.label: Lean proof of the preserved first hit

title: The distinct primes in a guessed repeat give a finite list of scales
impact: For 221 the false period guess 3 still gives a two-entry list, 1 and 3, which contains the successful square-root scale.
scope: For balanced primes, k supplied distinct prime divisors of the guess give exactly 2ᵏ scales when the list of divisors is complete. Obtaining that list has its own cost.
detail: The list contains a correct scale precisely when the squarefree part of the true shortest repeat divides the guess. The recovered pair then decides whether the guess itself repeats.

title: Two square roots and one gcd decide whether a guess is the shortest repeat
impact: Given 221, both 3 and 48 lead to the prime factors during the check. Recomputing the period rejects both guesses as the minimum and accepts 12.
scope: This exact equality test uses the product and a proposed length for two distinct primes at least seven. It takes one guess as input.
detail: A unit-power test accepts every multiple of the shortest repeat. The equality test reconstructs a candidate pair, verifies its product, and checks the exact reduced-predecessor product.

title: One square-root guess can succeed while the first period grows without bound
impact: On the constructed product 547,606,837, the very first square-root guess gives 22,501 and 24,337. The shortest shared repeat is 422,500.
scope: This is a special family with square totient. The finite formulas are checked in Lean. The infinitude argument applies a published theorem about fifty linear forms.
detail: For any prescribed period threshold, the construction admits pairs above it with q−p at least p/300. The direct calculation needs only the product and scale one.

title: A trillion square-root guesses still reach very few balanced pairs
impact: Fewer than one in 2⁷³⁶ eligible prime pairs yields its true sum at any square-root scale up to 2⁴⁰.
scope: The bound counts sorted distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. It applies to direct sum recovery, including successful guesses shorter than the first period.
detail: A successful scale forces the totient to be that scale times a square. Counting the possible square roots and divisors gives a finite estimate at the project’s actual input size.

title: A wrong guess for one sampled sequence can be rejected without summing it
impact: After two direct divisor checks, testing the odd-stride sequence reduces to powers of units. A failing power certifies failure at that specific starting offset.
scope: The reduction applies to odd primes p < q < 2p with the prescribed odd stride. It tests supplied guesses and relates the two shortest periods.
detail: At 221 the odd-stride sequence has period 24. Dividing by its common factor with the power of two removed from the stride gives 12, the shared period at stride 110.

title: A square-root test can find the primes before the first shared repeat
impact: On a constructed 2,048-bit product the square-root search split the number at guess 6. The shortest shared repeat, calculated from the recovered factors, had 2,043 bits.
scope: For distinct primes with 7 ≤ p < q ≤ 2p, the first correct square-root guess is the squarefree part of the shortest shared repeat. Finding that part cheaply for a general product remains open.
detail: The first guess is obtained by removing the largest square divisor from the repeat. We also characterize every later guess that recovers the sum. The 14,647 control was chosen for its square totient.

sources.label: Which period multiples recover the sum

title: One modular power can disprove a proposed shared repeat
impact: At 221, six steps repeat from one start. The remainder 118 from a single power of 3 proves six fails as a shared repeat.
scope: For two distinct primes at least seven and stride (N−1)/2, one failed test excludes the guess and all its divisors. A passing base can accept a wrong guess.
detail: Lean gives the exact fraction of units passing each guess. At length six exactly 96 of 192 units pass. Lengths 12 and 24 both pass for every unit.

title: Two reusable bases can test every proposed length
impact: At 221, bases 4 and 5 together accept exactly the multiples of 12. Two thirds of all ordered pairs there give correct answers to every guess.
scope: Two independently uniform units have a greater than 50% chance of being correct simultaneously for all guesses. Determining that a particular pair has this property is a separate task.
detail: The exact fraction is a product with one factor 1−1/ℓ² for each distinct prime ℓ dividing the shortest repeat. At 221 the factors for 2 and 3 give exactly two thirds.

title: A fixed list of small primes can settle a proposed repeat
impact: For a 2,048-bit product of two 1,024-bit primes, the prime bases through 2²¹ suffice to decide each shared-repeat guess under the published Dirichlet GRH estimate.
scope: The local proof takes a finite subgroup bound as a hypothesis. The cited paper supplies it under Dirichlet GRH. Selecting the shortest repeat is a separate search.
detail: A wrong guess has a proper subgroup of passing bases. The analytic result supplies a small prime outside that subgroup.

title: Even a trillion repeat guesses cover very few full-size products
impact: Fewer than one in 2⁹⁷⁸ eligible prime pairs has any positive shared repeat at most 2⁴⁰.
scope: The bound counts each sorted pair of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product once. It applies to the size of the shared repeat at stride (N−1)/2.
detail: The shortest length is a product of two coprime reduced predecessors. If it is small, both predecessors must lie in a short interval that can be counted explicitly.

title: One sampled sequence can encode the sum of balanced primes
impact: At 3,053, changing the stride shortened the repeat from 105 to 15 and gave the sum 114. At 221, removing a power of two from the stride corrected a misleading six-step repeat.
scope: For odd primes p < q < 2p, two direct divisor checks cover the exceptional cases. In the rest the exact shortest repeat at the specified odd stride gives the sum.
detail: Grouping terms reduced 77,070 updates to 210 at 3,053. Computing the groups still used all 3,053 residues, while Fermat's method found the same primes in two square tests.

sources.label: Lean proof for the single sequence

title: The shortest four-term rule determines the prime sum
impact: For 143 the shortest qualifying rule spans 11 even sums. Doubling the span and adding two gives 24, the sum of 11 and 13. Lean proves the general formula and its single exceptional ratio.
scope: The result applies to distinct same-width primes at least 11 and four invertible coefficients. The direct measurement on six small products used many sums. It encountered a factor earlier on all six.
detail: At 247 the exceptional span is 12 and the sum is 32. The quantity 24 × 247 + 1 is already the square of 77, which gives the factors 13 and 19 directly in this case.

title: Counting when two neighboring readings both vanish gives the prime sum
impact: At 77 there were exactly 19 such positions, giving the sum 18 and the factors 7 and 11. The same count at 221 gave 31 and recovered 13 and 17.
scope: The direct count takes one table entry per residue. Three related signs are easy to sample, but two fair coins and their product reproduce their distribution to within 2⁻⁹⁸⁰ over a trillion full-size draws.
detail: For every product of two distinct odd primes, the simultaneous-zero count is one plus their sum. We checked 526,786 positions across 276 small products.

title: The shortest recurrence for the even sums gives the larger prime exactly
impact: At 77 a rule reaching back four terms works forever, and every shorter rule fails. Doubling four and adding three gives the larger prime, 11.
scope: The formula works for any two distinct odd primes. For two 1,024-bit primes, the required order is at least 2¹⁰²². An inexpensive way to determine it from the product remains open.
detail: Eight even sums suffice to fit the rule at 77 if an order bound of four is supplied. The direct calculation of each sum uses all 77 residues.

sources.label: Lean exact order and finite-window proofs

title: At 77 the sums repeat after 30 degrees, exactly the unit-group exponent
impact: For primes at least seven, the smallest repeating shift gives the Carmichael function of their product. Taking only even degrees halves that period.
scope: The checker measured seven small products by summing every residue at successive degrees. Finding the period quickly from a large product remains open.
detail: The local sequence at prime 5 is constant. For 35 the even period is three, while half its Carmichael function is six.

sources.label: All seven measurements and the exceptions

title: Three terms can only compare even sums that already repeat
impact: For prime factors at least 11, every fixed three-term rule with invertible coefficients compares three identical values at different positions in the sequence.
scope: The rule must hold at every starting position. Its three offsets span at least two full periods. The distance between offsets is separate from the cost of evaluating a single sum.
detail: Four terms escape the restriction at 143. Offsets 0, 5, 6 and 11 satisfy an identity at every starting position, although the period is 30.

sources.label: Why sparse rules group their exponents

title: A fixed rule for predicting the even Jacobi sums must reach far back
impact: For 77, every fixed linear rule for all the even sums must reach back at least four terms. For two 1,024-bit primes the bound exceeds 2¹⁰²¹ terms.
scope: The bound applies to constant coefficients and a recurrence with leading coefficient one. Sparse long rules and direct ways to obtain a single chosen sum remain open.
detail: Even a rule that only fits the early even sums, before they reveal a prime, needs order at least floor((p − 3) / 4), where p is the smaller prime.

title: A trillion random signs look almost exactly like fair coin flips
impact: For two 1,024-bit primes, replacing up to 2⁴⁰ sampled Jacobi signs with independent fair coins changes the probability of any event on the signs by less than 2⁻⁹⁸¹.
scope: The calculation keeps only each sign from independent uniform draws. Retaining the chosen residues or selecting them adaptively gives a different experiment.
detail: At 77 the distribution is visibly uneven. It has 32 zeros, 23 plus signs and 22 minus signs. The exact distance after any number of draws is the chance of seeing at least one zero.

title: Rotating 42 sample points recovers the prime sum of 323
impact: Canceling one unwanted term gave the sum 36 and the factors 17 and 19. Across all 109 small products tested, the rotation recovered six.
scope: On every success, correcting an ordinary grid recovered the same factors with as many evaluations and fewer preparation steps. The evaluation itself used coefficients through the target.
detail: At 323 the rotation took 637 trial divisions to select. An ordinary grid with one subtraction took 26. Fermat found the factors in one square test.

title: Canceling three neighbors exactly still misses the coefficient of 527
impact: A signed reading canceled 528, 529 and 530. The rest of the series moved the answer at least 79 units below the target. Direct rounding to the known sum class has a tolerance of 12/527, about 0.023.
scope: The numerical enclosures cover three particular readings at 527. For one chosen neighbor, Lean proves the smallest possible error amplification given the frequency band and the log-distance to that neighbor.
detail: Canceling just 528 left an error between 60 and 93. The computation includes the first 5,000 terms and a bound on every later contribution.

title: The first degree where a Jacobi sum changes identifies the smaller prime
impact: For 77 the first change occurs at degree six, one less than the smaller prime, 7. Lean proves this location for every product of two distinct odd primes.
scope: Each degree summarizes a complete sum over the product's residue classes. Directly evaluating those sums and reaching the exceptional degree is expensive.
detail: Every lower degree has a known value modulo the product. At degree six the known value would be 20, while the measured value is 42 modulo 77.

title: Equally spaced samples mix the factor sum with much larger terms
impact: For 77 the desired coefficient is 18. With four sample points, a single earlier coefficient contributes 73,728 to the same reading.
scope: For an unrotated grid of up to 2⁴⁰ points on a 2,048-bit product, the earlier unwanted coefficient exceeds 2²⁰⁰⁵ even after all small divisor and cofactor contributions are removed through the stated cutoff.
detail: The proof uses the positive divisor-sum series and one circle of samples. Signed combinations of measurements from different circles are outside this bound.

title: The neighboring level 528 obscures a reading tuned to 527
impact: Even after removing the contributions of divisors up to 7, the contribution from 528 alone makes this positive average too inaccurate to round at any frequency height up to 527.
scope: For balanced 2,048-bit products and a divisor cutoff of 1,000, Lean rules out this averaging rule at heights through 2²⁰³⁷. Height measures the sampled frequency range.
detail: The exact coefficient at 527 is 49/527 after removing the small divisors. The nearby multiple of 11 contributes more than 1/22 of bias. Signed combinations can cancel contributions and require a separate analysis.

title: All prime-power samples can agree while the coefficient at 77 differs
impact: Two normalized modular forms of weight two and level 308 give identical coefficients at every prime power and give 96 and 97 at index 77.
scope: The example tests recovery from the level and sample values across the full space. A method specialized to a particular form can use further information.
detail: Every positive index that distinguishes the two forms is a multiple of 77. Knowing its complete factorization already gives 7 and 11. The same statement holds for any pair of distinct odd primes.

title: A modular curve gives the factor sum of 527
impact: The genus at level 2,108 was 283. It gives a factor sum of 48 and the primes 17 and 31.
scope: The relation holds for every product of two distinct odd primes. We computed the genus directly on this small example.
detail: Enumeration took 10,236 gcd tests. Test 106 had already exposed 17, and ordinary trial division reaches it in eight odd-divisor tests.

title: A square-root error bound would suffice at a larger level
impact: For a 2,048-bit product, one genus estimate at a 4,101-bit level would determine both factors if its error were at most the square root of that level.
scope: Lean checks the precision and recovery from the classical genus equation. A way to obtain such an estimate efficiently remains open.
detail: On the small product 15, increasing the level gave genera 17, 81 and 353. All three recover the same divisor sum. The cost of enumeration quadrupled at each step.

title: The average genus misses the necessary accuracy
impact: On every amplified level in the balanced 2,048-bit family, the published mean coefficient overestimates the genus by more than 2²⁰⁴⁰ times the square-root error target.
scope: This rules out applying the all-level average directly to an individual level. Other arithmetic estimates remain open.
detail: A second inexpensive estimate substitutes the first Fermat sum. It meets the target precisely on products where that first sum already gives both primes.

title: Four fixed directions distinguish two positive Jacobi symbols
impact: Two matrices modulo 77 both give a Jacobi symbol of +1. One preserves four directions and the other preserves none.
scope: For an odd semiprime and a matrix with invertible determinant and discriminant, an exact count detects whether the discriminant is a square modulo the product.
detail: The converse also holds. A general procedure to obtain these counts would decide quadratic residuosity. The proof identifies the missing information without supplying a fast count.

title: Powers of one matrix keep the same fixed directions until a scalar appears
impact: If a matrix power is nonscalar at both hidden primes, its fixed directions stay exactly the same at both primes.
scope: This covers every power of one invertible two-by-two matrix. Products of different matrices can change the directions.
detail: On 77, cubing a matrix raised the count from four to sixteen. Its entries already gave the divisor 7 before the count.

title: Even all 121 sums cover fewer than one prime pair in 2⁴⁹¹
impact: For two distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product, Lean bounded how often the true sum appears anywhere in the 121 candidates. Checking them all succeeds on a fraction between 2⁻⁵¹⁴ and 2⁻⁴⁹¹.
scope: This bound counts each eligible pair once and applies to these 121 sums. It holds even if the choice among them uses every bit of the product.
detail: A midpoint in the block forces the factors to differ by less than 2⁵¹⁷. The upper bound counts possible partners for each smaller prime. The lower bound groups primes into intervals short enough for every pair in a group to be covered.

title: A small table picks the same sum with fewer square roots
impact: On two 2,048-bit controls, the setup for selecting a sum fell from 25 and 49 input-dependent square roots to one apiece.
scope: Both controls stayed unfactored. The table used 4,097 small roots to build. The Python implementation took longer on both controls.
detail: With 14-bit primes and modulus 120, the larger table found 64,531 products versus 57,862 for Fermat at the same per-product root budget. The comparison counts 10.3 million table lookups separately. With the smaller table, Fermat recovered more.

title: One counted midpoint can rule out every later one
impact: An integer inequality lets the ranking stop as soon as later sums cannot fit more odd pairs. Both full-size examples needed only one midpoint count and three setup roots.
scope: It selects the same candidate as exact ranking. Both final factor checks missed.
detail: The full-size stopping check used three squares, one further large multiplication and a small-divisor division. On the two 66-bit examples it used two checks and cut the setup from 25 roots to five.

title: 121 sums suffice to find the most common sum for a word and remainder
impact: For a 2,048-bit product of two odd 1,024-bit integers, its upper half and remainder modulo 120 identify 121 sums worth comparing. One fits at least as many compatible integer pairs as any other sum.
scope: This ranks possible sums. The rule missed both 2,048-bit comparison products.
detail: Among 228,713 products of two 14-bit primes, ranking guessed correctly on 64,531. Ordinary Fermat search with the same remainder got 57,568 on its first guess and 192,183 with the ranking’s total square-root budget. Every successful ranked guess was covered at that budget.

title: One sum survives 52 candidates
impact: The surviving sum, 5,474, gives 2,293 × 3,181 from the product and the 12-bit factor width.
scope: One 23-bit product. Using the exact interval still left both 2,048-bit comparison products unfactored.
detail: The width bounds give 52 positions. Four pass the test modulo 63, and only one passes modulo 315. Constructing the table and its period takes 316 greatest-common-divisor calculations and 144 modular inversions before the final square test.

title: Two guesses find the most common sum among odd factor pairs
impact: Knowing only the upper half of the product bits, two row counts suffice to identify a sum shared by the most odd factor pairs.
scope: Proved for equal factor widths of at least 14 bits, including 1,024. The most common sum among prime pairs can be different.
detail: On 228,713 products of two 14-bit primes, ranking odd pairs gave 14,926 correct guesses. The first ordinary Fermat midpoint gave 17,324. The new rule found 83 that Fermat missed and missed 2,481 that Fermat found. Neither full-size control split.

title: Three quarters of the product bits still leave the sum hard to guess
impact: Even a list of 2⁴⁰ sums can cover fewer than one in 2⁴³⁴ eligible prime pairs if it sees only the top 1,024 bits and the bottom 512 bits.
scope: Uniformly chosen pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. A method using its middle 512 bits can use information outside this bound.
detail: Giving the rule the exact square-root ceiling, width quotients and remainder modulo 24 as well still keeps coverage below one in 2⁴²⁶. The proof counts pairs by how many times their difference can be divided by two.

title: Skipping multiples that cannot reveal the factors
impact: The product rules out at least 81% of the multiples in one complete difference-of-squares search.
scope: Every eligible 2,048-bit product still has more than 10¹⁰² qualifying multiples. A bounded trial on the fresh example fell from 11,328 square tests to 851 and missed.
detail: In one complete search for two unknown 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product, we can skip at least 81% of the trial multiples. More than 10¹⁰² different multiples still qualify on every such input. On our fresh example, the shorter search used 851 exact square tests down from 11,328 over the same bounded range. Both searches missed.

title: The same interval can fit many different prime sums
impact: For all but fewer than one pair in a billion, more than 2⁹⁰⁰ true sums occur among products that share the recorded data.
scope: Distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. The record includes the upper 1,024 product bits, the square-root ceiling, two quotients and the remainder modulo 24.
detail: Even a separately supplied 128-bit hint and a trillion candidate sums (up to 2⁴⁰) cover fewer than one in 2³⁹⁶ eligible pairs under this information model. An algorithm using other digits of the product to choose guesses falls outside the bound.

title: Three equations that cover every pair of primes above three
impact: At least one equation has a pair of solutions that reveals the factors. A bounded search split 22 of 32 fresh 40-bit inputs.
scope: For any two distinct primes above three. Locating the solutions still costs work. Five of 32 fresh 48-bit inputs split and both full-size comparisons remained unresolved.
detail: We can give three equations for any product of two different primes above three. One equation has solutions that reveal the factors. Finding them remains hard. The search split 22 of 32 fresh 40-bit numbers and five of 32 at 48 bits. Both 2,048-bit comparisons stayed unresolved.

title: At most one square test per proposed power
impact: The new stopping rule kept all 130 small factorizations while reducing square roots from 16,287 to 797.
scope: Across 12,994 small products with equal-width primes. The separate full-size trials found no factor.
detail: One square-root test per guess suffices for a search using continued fractions. Across 12,994 small products it kept all 130 factorizations and cut 16,287 square roots to 797. A separate run tried 106 guesses large enough to pass the division test on each of two 2,048-bit products and found neither pair.

title: When the first guess at the sum is enough
impact: The first even sum at or above twice the square root works on more than one in 2⁵¹⁷ eligible prime pairs.
scope: A guaranteed lower bound across the full 2,048-bit population. Close primes supply the successes, and the bound is too small to predict success on an individual input.
detail: The method tries even sums in increasing order. Counting primes that fall in the same short interval proves a success rate without assuming a random distribution of primes inside each short interval.

title: Two possible sums from 45 guesses
impact: A remainder test left 2,746 and 2,854 for 1,879,513. The second sum gave 1,031 × 1,823.
scope: A 45-position window on one small input. At full size, sums 20,160 apart can both pass somewhere at every modulus.
detail: Two guesses out of 45 survived the remainder tests for 1,879,513. The second gave 1,031 × 1,823. At 2,048 bits we proved a limit on the same idea. For every product, two guesses 20,160 apart can both pass somewhere, whatever modulus we choose.

title: Which extra fractions are worth checking?
impact: Including intermediate fractions found 118 of 903 small products, up from 78.
scope: All distinct pairs of 9-bit primes. On two 2,048-bit inputs, 106 guesses narrowed to 9 and 33 fractions without revealing a factor.
detail: A wider search found 118 of 903 small prime pairs, including 40 missed by the earlier version. It narrowed 106 guesses on each of two 2,048-bit products to 9 and 33 candidate fractions. Neither yielded a factor.

title: When adding a small number reveals the prime sum
impact: Trying 64 neighbors recovered 466 of 903 small products. Adding four to 108,671 gave the clue for 271 × 401.
scope: Even granting every divisor of the neighbors, this rule covers fewer than one in 2⁹⁷⁶ eligible 2,048-bit products.
detail: Adding four to 108,671 exposes a divisor that predicts the prime sum 672 and gives 271 × 401. Trying 64 nearby integers this way found 466 of 903 small products. At full size, even with every divisor available, fewer than one in 2⁹⁷⁶ eligible products can be recovered by that rule.

title: How often small prime powers can reveal the sum
impact: Exhausting the permitted powers can recover fewer than one in 2⁵⁵³ eligible 2,048-bit products.
scope: Applies to this continued-fraction rule, with exponents no greater than the product and all prime divisors at most 1,500.
detail: Could making more guesses find the two primes? For one method, suppose we try every number whose prime factors are all at most 1,500, stopping at the input number. This can recover the pair for fewer than one in 2⁵⁵³ balanced 2,048-bit products.

title: What an effective choice of exponent would reveal
impact: One exponent made a comparison succeed on three sevenths of the starting values for a 2,048-bit example.
scope: That exponent was chosen with the known factors. Five exponents chosen from the product gave no practical improvement.
detail: One power chosen with the known primes made a small set of comparisons succeed three times in seven on a 2,048-bit example. The proof explains what choosing such a power would require. Five powers computed from the product gave no practical improvement on this example.

title: Can a different starting value rescue a power comparison?
impact: On two 2,048-bit products, no starting value let cross-row comparisons find an additional factor.
scope: The proof used the published primes to check every starting value for this bounded comparison after its preliminary tests.
detail: Could a different starting number rescue a failed search? On two 2,048-bit examples we checked every possible starting number for one bounded search. Comparing powers across different rows could never add a factor after the preliminary checks. We used the known primes to establish that limit.

title: How far the multiplier search must go
impact: Only two multipliers work on each comparison product. The search passes at least 2⁵⁰¹ eligible multipliers before its first hit.
scope: Retrospective check using the published factors of two 2,048-bit products.
detail: We used the published factors to check exactly where one search would succeed on our two 2,048-bit examples. Only two multiples work on each input. Starting at one, the search must pass at least 2⁵⁰¹ eligible multiples before reaching the first answer.

scope: On the fresh 2,048-bit input, 64 blocks missed and a full traversal would take over 10²⁰⁶ blocks.

detail: Three clues from a 48-bit product let us jump over seven out of eight possible divisors. The number of divisions fell from 115,793 to 14,474. On both 2,048-bit inputs this calculation found no clue in its first 256 steps.

sources.label: Why there are at most two

title: A product-selected square test
impact: One square test recovered both factors of two specially constructed 2,048-bit products.
scope: It missed both comparison inputs. Even all multipliers in the family cover fewer than one in 2⁴⁸¹ balanced prime pairs at that size.
detail: One rule lets the product select a single square test. It recovered both primes on two constructed 2,048-bit numbers and missed on both earlier comparison numbers. Even testing every multiplier in this family covers fewer than one in 2⁴⁸¹ balanced prime pairs at this size.

title: A product-selected filter for square tests
impact: On the fresh 2,048-bit input, the filter reduced about 42 billion survivors to 19 billion among a trillion choices.
scope: Testing 64 survivors per version found no full-size factor. A smaller example split at adjustment 13.
detail: A broader square test found 36,559 × 64,997 at adjustment 13. On the fresh 2,048-bit number, selecting the filter from the product cut the survivors from roughly 42 billion to 19 billion out of a trillion choices. Testing 64 survivors in each version yielded no factor.

title: Using the factor sum to remove groups
impact: The sum bounds reduced the number of groups fourfold on the fresh 2,048-bit product. A later test excluded 2,048 groups together in 0.76 seconds.
scope: These exclusions left both full-size factors unknown to the search.
detail: On the fresh 2,048-bit example, using the possible sums of the two primes cut the number of groups to search by a factor of four. A later test ruled out 2,048 of those groups together in 0.76 seconds. This search has not recovered either of the two primes used to build the example.

sources.label: Fresh result, Lean exclusion proof and remaining work

title: Testing a guess for one factor remainder
impact: A single guess recovered the two 1,024-bit primes of the crossed control in 2.21 seconds.
scope: The original guess used the published factors. Fixed in advance, it succeeded on three of ten constructed inputs and missed a fresh product.
detail: One guess recovered both 1,024-bit primes of our earlier comparison number in 2.21 seconds. We chose it after seeing the published factors. Testing the same guess using only the products succeeded on three of ten constructed examples and missed the other seven. It also missed a fresh product generated after we fixed the guess.

sources.label: See the two primes and Lean certificate

title: Checking four groups with one equation
impact: In a successful group the equation leaves at most four possible factors. Finite differences cut the complete count by another 43% in a matched comparison.
scope: The count of groups on the fresh 2,048-bit input still has 184 decimal digits.
detail: One equation now checks four of the original groups at once. If we choose the right group, it leaves at most four possible factors. On our 2,048-bit test number, using these equations cut the number of groups by a factor of about 64 quintillion compared with our earlier linear search. Checking positive and negative solutions together almost halved the count again. Using finite differences cut the complete count a further 43% in a matched comparison. On the fresh product, using the difference between the factors cut another 29% compared with ordinary Newton equations. The number of groups still has 184 digits.

sources.label: How finite differences reduce the search

title: One weighted sum for a group of factor pairs
impact: Complete searches on eight fresh 49–50-bit inputs took 0.058 seconds in total, compared with 1.003 seconds for trial division in the same intervals.
scope: At 2,048 bits a complete search still requires more than 2⁶⁷⁶ groups.
detail: One weighted sum can check an entire group of factor pairs. On 34,387, four groups led to a single sum and the factors 137 and 251. Across eight fresh 49–50-bit inputs, the complete search took 0.058 seconds, compared with 1.003 seconds for trial division over the same intervals. A complete search by this rule still needs more than 2⁶⁷⁶ groups at 2,048 bits.

sources.label: Grouping related checks on an 82-bit input

title: Choosing a base to reduce candidate pairs
impact: Changing the base cut the number of pairs checked from 4,478 to 1,853 across eight fresh inputs. Both searches recovered every pair.
scope: Trial division was faster on all eight, and the 2,048-bit search still exceeds 2⁶⁸⁰ groups.
detail: Changing the base used to write the two unknown factors cut the candidate pairs checked from 4,478 to 1,853 across eight fresh products. Both searches found every pair. Ordinary trial division was faster on all eight inputs. At 2,048 bits the new search would still visit more than 2⁶⁸⁰ groups.

title: Wrong midpoints that survive prime-power tests
impact: For every target-size product, more than 2⁸⁷⁴ wrong midpoints survive all powers of all primes through 733.
scope: Local tests can isolate the answer on small inputs. Powers of 2, 3 and 5 isolated the midpoint for 34,387.
detail: On 34,387, tests at powers of 2, 3 and 5 left exactly one possible midpoint for the primes. It gave 137 and 251. On our 2,048-bit comparison input, three prime-power tests eliminated 99.126% of the interval and still left a 1,013-bit count of possibilities. Even at every power of every prime through 733, more than 2⁸⁷⁴ wrong midpoints survive on every target-size product.

title: Narrower intervals for weighted sums
impact: On one 89-bit product the search fell from 14.18 to 1.34 seconds. It also factored a fresh 99-bit product in 7.59 seconds.
scope: GNU factor took 0.325 seconds on the 99-bit input. A full 2,048-bit search needs more than 2⁴⁰⁴ records.
detail: Narrowing the possible sums of two weighted factors recovered both primes of a fresh 99-bit number in 7.59 seconds. GNU’s factor utility took 0.325 seconds on that number. On the same 89-bit input, the previous full-interval search took 14.18 seconds and this search took 1.34 seconds. On the 2,048-bit control, 96 blocks yielded no factor. A full search with these windows would need more than 2⁴⁰⁴ records.

title: Reading a prime as a sum of squares
impact: Two character sums can encode a prime as a sum of squares. On 26,441 the readings gave 11 and 4, recovering 137.
scope: Both primes must be 1 modulo 4 for this result. The example required 26,440 symbol evaluations.
detail: For products whose primes both leave remainder 1 when divided by 4, two sums encode a prime as a sum of two squares. On 26,441 we recovered 11 and 4, whose squares add to 137. Calculating the two sums still took 26,440 symbol evaluations.

title: Recovering a factor from a sum over pairs
impact: On 77 a sum over pairs equals 21. Adding one and dividing by two gives the prime 11 even though both ordinary sums vanish.
scope: Directly evaluating the pair sum took 5,929 positions on this small input.
detail: Both ordinary sums vanish on 77. A sum over pairs gives 21, so (21 + 1) / 2 recovers 11. The same approach extends to other prime pairs. Computing the sum directly on 77 took 5,929 positions.

sources.label: Why the formula works and how the cost grows

title: Charging the cost of filtering possible divisors
impact: Remainder compatibility reduced 83,891 possible divisors to 16,908 on a 41-bit input.
scope: The complete search took eight times longer once it included the work of applying the filter.
detail: On a 41-bit input, checking whether candidate factors have compatible remainders cut 83,891 possible divisors to 16,908. The complete search took eight times longer once we counted the work of excluding candidates.

title: Three expressions for the smaller prime
impact: For any two distinct odd primes, one of three expressions yields the smaller one. On 713 a final gcd gives 23.
scope: Computing that gcd's input is expensive. With two 1,024-bit primes, searching both coordinates only up to 2⁵¹⁰ cannot succeed.
detail: For any product of two distinct odd primes, one of three simple expressions equals its smaller prime. On 713 our formula returns 23 in one greatest common divisor calculation. The work goes into the product used in that calculation. For two 1,024-bit primes, checking even the full range up to 2⁵¹⁰ in both coordinates finds nothing.

title: A smaller-coordinate search against direct division
impact: The search recovered 2,423,330,473 and 2,513,756,873 on a fresh 63-bit product.
scope: Searching the possible odd divisors directly was faster on the same input.
detail: On a fresh 63-bit input, the smaller-coordinate search found 2,423,330,473 and 2,513,756,873. A direct search of the possible odd divisors was faster on this input.

title: How often weighted sums of squares reveal factors
impact: At most 132 weights and 849 multiples per weight suffice to contain two revealing solutions for all but fewer than one in 2¹¹⁹ of the specified prime pairs.
scope: The probability is over uniform distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. The full-size comparison exhausted its budget searching for the solutions.
detail: From a 2,048-bit product we can select at most 132 weights for a sum of two squares and try up to 849 multiples of the product per weight. For two uniformly chosen distinct 1,024-bit primes giving a product of this size, fewer than one pair in 2¹¹⁹ lacks two revealing solutions in this search. Finding those solutions is still expensive. On a small example we started with 3,599 and found 59 and 61. Our 2,048-bit comparison exhausted its search budget.

title: Changing the polynomial during a search
impact: At the same search budget, changing polynomials factored six of 16 fresh 79-bit products. One ordinary interval found no factors.
scope: The comparison measures this fixed sample and budget.
detail: On the same 16 fresh 79-bit products, one ordinary interval found no factors at its fixed budget. Changing the polynomial at regular intervals found both primes on six inputs.

title: Finding factors from short fractions
impact: Checking 24 multiples recovered both primes of a 2,048-bit product constructed to have a short usable fraction.
scope: On the second full-size product 57,769 square roots exhausted the reduced search. Every successful pair of fractions was outside its range.
detail: We found both primes of a specially constructed 2,048-bit number after checking 24 of its multiples. On a second number of the same size, a faster search cut over two million square roots to 57,769 and exhausted its range. We proved that every working pair of fractions on this second number exceeds that range.

title: The chance of drawing two useful fractions together
impact: Two fractions from the same draw split 77,837 on the seventeenth try.
scope: For a target-size product, even 281 trillion random tries have probability below 2⁻⁷⁴⁸ of producing the required pair under the stated sampling rule.
detail: Two fractions from the same draw can guarantee a factor. Our search found such a pair for 77,837 on its seventeenth try and recovered 277 and 281. For a 2,048-bit product of two 1,024-bit primes, even 281 trillion random tries have less chance of producing such a pair than 748 fair coins have of all landing heads.

sources.label: See the example and sampling assumptions

title: Trading more fraction checks for fewer draws
impact: Trying all proportions recovered a sampled 79-bit product in 70,166 draws, down from 1,211,456.
scope: Testing more fractions per draw increased the total CPU time on that input.
detail: Writing a square remainder as a fraction split a sampled 79-bit product. Trying all proportions needed 70,166 draws, down from 1,211,456. Checking more fractions took more CPU time on this input. At 2,048 bits we can bound how rarely these searches yield a usable row.

title: Scoring continued-fraction multipliers from the product
impact: At a fixed step limit, a product-based multiplier choice raised successes from 14 to 26 among 64 fresh 79-bit products.
scope: The comparison establishes a gain on those small products. The score can miss useful multipliers at 2,048 bits.
detail: Using the product to choose a starting multiplier improved a continued-fraction search on a fresh sample. It found both primes in 26 of 64 cases, up from 14 at the same step limit. All the products in that comparison had 79 bits.

sources.label: Why the score can fail at 2,048 bits

title: Combining small remainders across a fresh sample
impact: Combining remainders split 13 of 64 fresh 79-bit products. Continued fractions split 15, with 12 successes in common.
scope: On a 2,048-bit product more than four billion classes gave 58 small remainders. None of their combinations revealed a factor.
detail: On 64 fresh 79-bit products, combining small remainders recovered both primes in 13 cases. Continued fractions succeeded in 15, with 12 successes in common. On a 2,048-bit test, we searched more than four billion possible classes and found 58 small remainders. No combination of those 58 gave a factor.

title: A full-size split from related prime orders
impact: A search given only the product recovered both primes on its thirteenth try in a constructed 2,048-bit example.
scope: One prime plus one divided the other prime squared minus one. After replacing one prime, the same thirteen tries found nothing.
detail: We built a 2,048-bit example where one prime plus one divides the other prime squared minus one. A search given only the product found both primes on its thirteenth try. We then replaced just one prime. The product was still 2,048 bits, and the same thirteen tries found nothing.

title: Grouping quotient intervals by residue modulo six
impact: Grouping the balanced interval for 1,900,014,700,027 cut the search from 5,111 strips to 1,708 and recovered 1,000,003 and 1,900,009.
scope: This is a complete comparison on one small product. The method still searches multiple strips.
detail: A search of the full balanced range for 1,900,014,700,027 took 1,708 strips when we grouped factors by their remainders modulo 6, down from 5,111. It recovered the primes 1,000,003 and 1,900,009. On 77,837, three unsuccessful divisor checks together revealed 277 and 281.

title: Recognizing the correct midpoint with random checks
impact: Among distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product, 1,040 random checks identify the midpoint with probability above 99.9999% when every candidate is tested.
scope: The checks still require a candidate search. The 41-bit example tested all 41,807 possibilities.
detail: For two distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product, 1,040 random checks can identify their average with over 99.9999% probability if we test every candidate. On a 41-bit example, we tested all 41,807 candidates to find the one that passed.

title: A binomial remainder that gives the larger prime
impact: For odd primes p < q < 4p, a binomial remainder determined by their product gives the larger prime exactly.
scope: This covers any two distinct 1,024-bit primes. Direct evaluation already needed a 761,262-bit intermediate on a 31-bit product. Efficient full-size evaluation remains open.
detail: For 143 = 11 × 13, the chosen coefficient leaves remainder 12, revealing the larger prime 13. The ratio condition q < 4p is essential to the stated guarantee.

title: Recovering the factors from one rounded value
impact: On 32 full-size products a value accurate to 1,366 fractional bits gave both primes with one square test.
scope: Known primes supplied the full-size values. A smaller value was computed directly for 60,491, recovering 241 and 251.
detail: On 32 full-size products, one value rounded to 1,366 fractional bits let us recover both primes with one square test. We used known primes to generate each value. We also computed a shorter value directly from 60,491 and recovered 241 and 251. Finding a cheap way to compute it at full size remains open.

sources.label: How many bits suffice on average?

title: When a continued fraction reveals a planted relation
impact: Removing a multiplier revealed both factors of a constructed 2,048-bit product in four steps.
scope: The input had a close match between small multiples of its primes. A multiplier of 133 exhausted 65,536 steps on the same number.
detail: On the same specially constructed 2,048-bit product, a search using a multiplier of 133 exhausted 65,536 steps. Removing the multiplier revealed both primes at the fourth step. The input was built with a close match between two small multiples of its primes.

title: Combining rounded sums to recover remainders
impact: One precision schedule uses 89 sums with 53 fractional bits each. On 667, one 616-term sum sufficed to recover 23 and 29.
scope: The setup for the small example also encounters its factors. Higher precision in one sum can supply several readings.
detail: An alternative uses 89 sums rounded to 53 fractional bits each. A higher-precision sum can supply several readings. For 667 we used one sum of 616 terms to recover 23 and 29. Its setup also encounters the factors.

title: A wide-modulus sieve and its full-size cost
impact: The proposed worst-case bound excludes more guesses for similarly sized primes. The search recovered both primes of a randomly drawn 79-bit product.
scope: The full bound awaits independent review. At 2,048 bits the main sieve requires at least 2⁴⁰⁰ residue visits or table entries.
detail: For two similarly sized primes, we derive a way to rule out more guesses. The full bound awaits independent review. The search recovered both primes of a 79-bit product from random prime draws. At 2,048 bits the main sieve requires at least 2⁴⁰⁰ residue visits or table entries.

sources.label: Read the bound and its assumptions

title: Even a correct digit can leave many candidate sums
impact: At least 2⁶³⁰ sums on the fresh product and 2⁶³³ on the crossed product pass both the supplied digit and the remainder test.
scope: Two specific 2,048-bit inputs. The digit radix is at most 2¹²⁸ and the combined sieve modulus at most 2²⁵⁶. The correct digit is supplied for free.
detail: A true sum passes once in each complete repetition of its digit and sieve pattern. The proof counts distinct survivors inside the actual interval without assuming any of these other candidates have an integer-square discriminant.

title: One large-prime test leaves about half the sums
impact: Between 43.75% and 56.25% of the first 2⁵²¹ candidates in the tested progression pass.
scope: One 2,048-bit product and an independent 1,024-bit test prime. The count uses two published analytic estimates as explicit hypotheses.
detail: A surviving sum has a square discriminant modulo the chosen prime. Locating a sum with an integer-square discriminant remains a separate problem. The bound counts the survivors without scanning the window.
